title: Design a URL Shortener (bit.ly) — System Design Case Study
summary: End-to-end design of a bit.ly-style URL shortener: requirements and scale estimates, short code generation (base62, counters, hashing, collisions), redirect semantics (301 vs 302), custom aliases and expiry, analytics, read-heavy caching, and scaling and failure handling.

chapters.title: URL Shortener Case Study Cover
points: Scope and requirements
High-level architecture
Short code generation
Redirect service 301 vs 302
Custom aliases and expiry
Click analytics pipeline
Read-heavy caching
Scaling, failures, interview Qs

chapters.title: Problem Statement, Scope and Requirements (URL Shortener)
points: Scope: create short link, redirect, custom alias, expiry, click analytics; out of scope: user auth UI, link previews, spam ML
Functional: POST long URL returns short URL; GET short code redirects; alias optional; TTL optional (default 5 years)
Non-functional: redirect p99 under 50 ms, 99.99% availability on reads, created links never change target
Writes: 100M new URLs per month is about 40 writes/s average, about 400/s at 10x peak
Reads: 100:1 read-to-write ratio gives 10B redirects per month, about 4,000 QPS average, about 40,000 QPS peak
Storage: 500 bytes per record x 100M/month x 12 x 5 years = 3 TB; cache 20% of daily 350M redirects: 70M x 500 B = about 35 GB in RAM

chapters.title: High-Level Architecture (URL Shortener)
points: Components: load balancer, stateless API servers, ID generator, cache (Redis), primary DB, async analytics queue
Write path: client to API to ID generator to base62 encode to DB insert to return short URL
Read path: client to LB to cache lookup; on miss read DB, fill cache, return redirect
Separate read service from write service: reads scale at 100x writes and need different autoscaling
Stateless servers behind LB: any node serves any code, so horizontal scaling needs no sticky sessions

chapters.title: Short Code Generation: Base62 and Length (URL Shortener)
points: Base62 alphabet: 0-9, a-z, A-Z gives 62 symbols per character; avoid +/ of base64 because they are URL-unsafe
Length math: 62^6 = 56.8B codes, 62^7 = 3.52T codes; 7 chars covers 100M/month for 5 years (6B URLs) with large headroom
Encode: repeatedly divide integer ID by 62, map remainders to alphabet, reverse; ID 125 becomes '21' (2x62+1)
Codes must be unique, short, and non-guessable if links are private; sequential base62 leaks creation order and volume
Metric: code length distribution and keyspace used percentage; alert at 50% of 62^7 used

chapters.title: Code Strategies: Counter vs Hash vs Random (URL Shortener)
points: Hash approach: MD5/SHA-256 of long URL, take first 7 base62 chars; stateless but collisions grow past ~1M links (birthday bound)
Collision handling for hash: check DB on insert, on conflict append a salt or counter and rehash; costs an extra read per write
Counter approach: global auto-increment to base62; zero collisions, but needs a distributed counter and is guessable
Pre-generated key service (KGS): offline-generated unique 7-char keys in used/unused tables; API fetches a batch of 1,000 keys into memory
Counter ranges: ZooKeeper or DB hands each app server a block of 1M IDs; a crashed server wastes at most its unused block
Comparison: hash = dedup-friendly but collision retries; counter = collision-free but predictable; KGS = unique and random-looking but extra service to run
Mistake: using random 7 chars without a unique constraint; the DB unique index on short_code is the final collision guard

chapters.title: Redirect Service: 301 vs 302 (URL Shortener)
points: GET /{code}: look up long URL, respond with 3xx and Location header; unknown code returns 404, expired returns 410 Gone
301 Moved Permanently: browsers and CDNs cache it, so repeat clicks skip your server; cuts load but analytics lose those clicks
302 Found (temporary): every click hits your server; full analytics and ability to change or expire the target; higher load
Choice: products with analytics and expiry use 302 (or 307), or a 301 with a short private max-age as Bitly does; pure-SEO permanent links use 301
Cache-Control max-age on a 301 is hard to undo; a wrongly-cached permanent redirect stays in browsers for months
Metrics: redirect p50/p99 latency, 4xx rate, cache hit ratio above 95%, redirect QPS

chapters.title: Custom Aliases and Link Expiry (URL Shortener)
points: POST /v1/urls body {long_url, custom_alias?, expires_at?}; returns 201 with short_url, 409 if alias taken
Alias rules: 4-30 chars, [A-Za-z0-9_-], reserved words blocked (api, admin, login); case-sensitive
Alias uniqueness: same unique index on short_code; insert-or-fail is atomic, no check-then-insert race
Table urls: short_code PK, long_url, user_id, created_at, expires_at; 500 bytes per row
Lazy expiry: check expires_at on read and return 410; plus a daily batch job deletes expired rows and recycles keys
Failure: two users claim the same alias concurrently; unique constraint lets one win and the other gets 409

chapters.title: Click Analytics Pipeline (URL Shortener)
points: Never write analytics on the redirect path: publish a click event {code, ts, ip, user_agent, referrer} to Kafka asynchronously
Consumers aggregate into a column store (ClickHouse) with counts per code per minute, country, device
Volume: 40,000 clicks/s peak x ~200 bytes = 8 MB/s, and 10B clicks/month x 200 B = about 2 TB per month raw; keep raw 30 days, rollups forever
GET /v1/urls/{code}/stats?range=7d returns total clicks, clicks by day, top countries, top referrers
Failure: Kafka down must not break redirects; fire-and-forget with bounded buffer, accept losing some clicks
Metrics: event lag under 10 s, drop rate, consumer throughput, bot traffic filtered by user-agent

chapters.title: Read-Heavy Caching Layer (URL Shortener)
points: Cache-aside: read Redis key code to long_url; on miss read DB and set with TTL; writes also populate cache
Sizing: 20% of daily 350M redirects hot, 70M x 500 B = 35 GB, fits one Redis cluster of 3 shards
Eviction: LRU with maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru; per-key TTL capped at link expiry
Failure: cache stampede on a viral link; use request coalescing or a lock so one request refills the key
Failure: negative caching of 404s for 60 s stops attackers scanning random codes from hammering the DB
Add CDN or edge cache for 301 or hot 302 targets; target hit ratio above 95%, miss path under 10 ms DB read

chapters.title: Database Design and Sharding (URL Shortener)
points: Access pattern is pure key-value lookup by short_code, so NoSQL (DynamoDB, Cassandra) or sharded SQL both fit
Shard by hash(short_code) with consistent hashing; avoids range hot spots from sequential IDs
3 TB over 5 years at 1 TB per node: 3 shards would be 100% full, so plan about 6 shards at ~50% fill, each with 2 replicas (18 nodes)
Replication: async read replicas serve redirects; primary only takes writes at about 400/s
Failure: shard loss handled by replica promotion; replication lag can make a fresh link 404, so read primary after create
Metrics: replication lag under 1 s, shard size skew, disk usage, p99 query latency

chapters.title: Scaling, Failures, Trade-offs and Interview Questions (URL Shortener)
points: Scale path: stateless API autoscaling, Redis cluster, DB read replicas, CDN, then shard; 40,000 QPS peak needs about 10 API nodes at 4,000 QPS each
Multi-region: active-active reads with regional caches; writes to a home region with key ranges per region to avoid ID clashes
Abuse: rate limit creation at 100 URLs/hour per user, scan targets against malware lists, block redirect loops
Trade-off table: 301 vs 302, hash vs counter vs KGS, SQL vs NoSQL, strong vs eventual consistency on new links
Interview Qs: how to avoid collisions at 100M/month; how to count clicks without slowing redirects; what if the cache dies; how to make codes unguessable
Interview Q: how do you delete or expire a link already cached in a CDN or browser (answer: use 302 or short max-age)

chapters.title: URL Shortener Cheatsheet
points: Estimates: 40 writes/s, 4,000 reads/s avg, 40,000 peak, 3 TB in 5 years, 7-char base62 = 3.52T codes
Redirect: 302 for analytics and expiry, 301 for permanent cached; 404 unknown, 410 expired, 409 alias taken
Code gen: KGS or counter ranges for uniqueness; hash needs collision retry; unique index is the last guard
Cache-aside Redis LRU, hit ratio above 95%, negative cache 404s, coalesce stampedes
Analytics async via Kafka to ClickHouse; never block the redirect path
